name: Aluminum chloride prescription (Drysol)
lead: Drysol is a brand of prescription topical aluminium chloride solution used for hyperhidrosis, or excessive sweating.[1] People use it for a presentation payoff: less visible sweat on underarms, hands, feet or face means fewer sweat stains on clothes, drier handshakes and a neater look through the day. Aluminium chloride is a higher-strength relative of the ingredient in over-the-counter antiperspirants, and guidelines summarized on Wikipedia list high-concentration aluminium chloride products as first-line therapy.[1]

Aluminium salts react with the electrolytes in sweat to form a gel plug in the sweat-gland duct, which is slowly shed as the skin sloughs.[2] Wikipedia reports that improvement takes about three to five days and that the most common side effect is skin irritation.[1] Case reports describe 20% aluminium chloride in alcohol (Drysol) used for localized sweating, including a woman with one-sided segmental hyperhidrosis and a patient with facial and scalp sweating treated with it alongside an oral medicine.[4][5] Hyperhidrosis is described in the dermatology literature as a psychosocially embarrassing condition.[3]

Training forums such as T Nation have threads in which lifters ask about heavy sweating and share what they use, including moisture-wicking clothing and, in one thread, a link to consumer information on prescription aluminium chloride.[6][7][8]

paras: Drysol is the best-known brand name of an aluminium chloride solution made in an alcohol base for use on the skin. It sits between consumer antiperspirants, which are sold over the counter, and procedural treatments such as injections or devices. In the United States the FDA classifies antiperspirant deodorants as drugs, and it advises people with kidney disease to consult a doctor before using aluminium-containing antiperspirants.[2]

The case literature uses 20% aluminium chloride in alcohol as the reference strength for Drysol.[5] A 1977 Medical Letter review titled 'Drysol for treatment of hyperhidrosis' is among the earliest clinical summaries of the product.[9]

Hyperhidrosis is sweating beyond what the body needs to regulate temperature. Focal hyperhidrosis may affect up to 2.8% of the US population, affects men and women equally, most often appears between ages 25 and 64, and has a family history in 30 to 50 percent of cases.[1] More than 80% of patients are reported to experience moderate to severe emotional effects.[1]

Wikipedia describes high-concentration aluminium chloride solutions or gels as first-line therapy, working especially well for the underarms, with improvement in about three to five days.[1] Higher-strength aluminium chloride antiperspirants have shown some success for hand and foot sweating.[1] Other options listed for people who need more than topical treatment include tap-water iontophoresis, botulinum toxin A injections (effects lasting roughly 3 to 9 months), oral anticholinergics such as glycopyrrolate and oxybutynin, and surgical options.[1]

The appearance payoff is indirect but concrete: sweat marks, damp collars, shiny skin and wet palms are visible in photos and in person. The yellow stains that some antiperspirant formulations can leave on clothing are a separate issue that some people address with underarm liners.[2] Lifters on T Nation describe heavy sweating during and after training and discuss clothing choices and medical options for it.[6][7][8]

Beyond underarm sweating, Drysol has been reported for palmar and plantar sweating,[1] localized one-sided sweating,[5] and facial and scalp sweating in combination with oral clonidine in a single case report.[4] Dermatologists have also used aluminium chloride (Drysol) as a hemostatic agent in minor surgical procedures.[10]

Aluminium salts used in antiperspirants react with electrolytes in sweat to form a gel plug within the duct of the sweat gland. The plugs are gradually removed as the skin sheds, which is why the effect wears off and applications are repeated. The salts also have a mild astringent effect that narrows pores.[2]
The 1978 case report of one-sided segmental hyperhidrosis paired 20% aluminium chloride with plastic wrap over the treated area, an occlusion approach described in the dermatology literature.[5]
Skin irritation is the most common side effect.[1] The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminium antiperspirants.[2]

A 1978 case report described miliaria (heat rash) with exertion after repeated use of 20% aluminium chloride in a patient with segmental hyperhidrosis.[5] A 1993 report described an unusual histiocytic reaction in skin biopsies after topical aluminium chloride used as a hemostatic agent, termed a 'Drysol reaction'.[10]

Public concern about aluminium antiperspirants has centered on breast cancer and Alzheimer's disease. Wikipedia notes the breast cancer idea spread widely after a 1999 chain email; it reports no supporting evidence, while the US National Cancer Institute has said studies gave conflicting results. A 2014 review of 469 studies found little evidence that exposure to metallic aluminium, its oxides or its salts raises Alzheimer's risk.[2] The EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety, in 2020, considered aluminium compounds safe at up to 6.25% in non-spray products and 10.60% in spray products; those limits apply to consumer cosmetics rather than prescription solutions.[2]

Antiperspirants have a longer history than Drysol. Edna Murphey of Philadelphia developed Mum, the first modern commercial deodorant, in 1888, and Everdry became the first commercial antiperspirant in 1903.[2] Jules Montenier patented the modern antiperspirant formulation in 1941, first used in Stopette, and Ban Roll-On arrived in 1952.[2]

Botulinum toxin was first used for sweating in 1993, and tap-water iontophoresis for palms and soles dates to the 1950s, giving later options for people who need more than aluminium salts.[1] Published Drysol-specific material includes the 1977 Medical Letter review and case reports from the late 1970s onward.[9][5]

Published Drysol-specific work consists mainly of case reports,[4][5] a 1977 Medical Letter review,[9] and a 2005 dermatopathology review that lists the Drysol reaction among tissue changes that can mimic infection under the microscope.[11] The Hyperhidrosis article on Wikipedia summarizes guidelines that recommend topical aluminium chloride first, citing an evidence-based review of nonsurgical management and guidance from the International Hyperhidrosis Society.[1] One cited trial of tap-water iontophoresis reported roughly 80% sweat reduction, and a case report on botulinum toxin for inguinal hyperhidrosis lists aluminium-salt antiperspirants such as Drysol among earlier treatments of varied success.[1][3]

sections.h: Use in training and grooming communities
paras: On T Nation, a 2001 thread titled 'Sweating Part 2' includes a reply explaining that soaking through a shirt in minutes in a cool gym may indicate axillary hyperhidrosis and listing several ways to treat it.[8] A 2006 thread describes loose moisture-wicking shirts as the one measure the poster found helpful,[6] and a 2009 thread on underarm sweat includes a link to consumer information about aluminium chloride topical solution (Drysol, Xerac AC).[7]

The Medical Letter publishes a review of Drysol for hyperhidrosis.[9]
Case report of 20% aluminium chloride with plastic wrap for one-sided segmental hyperhidrosis.[5]

lore.intro: Drysol appears in lifting and grooming forums as one answer to heavy sweating, alongside clothing choices.[6][7][8]

claims.claim: Moisture-wicking, loose shirts are the main thing that helps with heavy sweating
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says most of their wardrobe is moisture-wicking and that this is the only thing they found to actually help.[6]
claims.experts: Dermatology summaries list aluminium chloride antiperspirants as first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis, with other options when they are insufficient; clothing is not a listed treatment.[1]

claims.claim: Heavy sweating that soaks a shirt in minutes may be a medical condition with treatments
claims.believers: A T Nation reply states that soaking through a shirt quickly in an air-conditioned gym may be axillary hyperhidrosis and that there are several ways to treat it.[8]
claims.experts: Focal hyperhidrosis may affect up to 2.8% of the US population and is treated with aluminium chloride, iontophoresis, botulinum toxin, oral anticholinergics or surgery.[1]

card.summary: Rx aluminium chloride for heavy sweating; first-line, mainly irritating.
card.note: Skin irritation is the most common side effect.

quick.overview:
Drysol is a prescription aluminium chloride solution used for hyperhidrosis. It is a stronger form of the ingredient in ordinary antiperspirants.

Topical antiperspirants are guideline first-line treatment.
quick.mechanism: Aluminium salts block sweat ducts, reducing sweat output.
quick.risks: Skin irritation is the most common effect. Kidney dysfunction warrants a doctor consult per the FDA.

chain: Aluminium salts applied to sweat-prone skin
Sweat output at that site is reduced
Fewer sweat stains and less damp skin
angle.text: The solution reduces sweating where it is applied, which people use to avoid visible underarm marks, wet hands or a shiny face. The effect is on sweat rather than skin or body features.
